case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2)’s requirement that the Veterans Court “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error” obligates that court to conduct an issue-specific harmless-error analysis (considering the case’s circumstances) or permits it to deem certain Veterans Affairs notice/duty-to-assist errors categorically harmless without that inquiry.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 7261(a)–(b), especially § 7261(b)(2) (the Veterans Court’s scope of review and its duty to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Federal Circuit has allowed the Veterans Court to short-circuit § 7261(b)(2) by treating some VA errors—particularly those involving required notice or assistance obligations—as automatically nonprejudicial based on broad assumptions rather than evaluating whether the error affected the individual veteran’s ability to develop evidence, present arguments, or obtain benefits in the particular case. They contend the statute’s text (“take due account”) and this Court’s administrative-law harmless-error principles require a contextual, case-by-case prejudice inquiry, and that categorical rules improperly shift burdens to veterans and undermine the pro-claimant nature of the veterans benefits system.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Secretary argues that the Veterans Court and Federal Circuit are correctly applying the “rule of prejudicial error” in a manner consistent with ordinary harmless-error doctrine: not every procedural misstep warrants remand, and courts may affirm when the record shows the veteran was not harmed. The government contends petitioners are effectively seeking a more rigid remand rule than § 7261(b)(2) allows, that the challenged decisions reflect permissible applications of harmless-error review (including reliance on record-based indicators that an error made no difference), and that the Federal Circuit’s approach does not create the kind of categorical, across-the-board rule petitioners describe.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2) imports ordinary harmless-error principles and does not mandate remand for every defect, and I accept Justice Alito’s warning against recreating an automatic-remand regime. But Sanders’s emphasis on a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record” forecloses the Veterans Court from disposing of prejudice through a categorical rule that an entire class of notice/duty-to-assist errors is harmless without testing that conclusion against the particular record. Kotteakos’s substantial-influence/grave-doubt framework similarly requires a record-anchored assessment of whether the error could have mattered here, even if that assessment is often brief where harmlessness is clear. A narrow vacatur and remand requiring an issue- and record-specific harmless-error analysis respects Thomas’s textual point while enforcing Sanders’s prohibition on rigid presumptions—whether pro- or anti-remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s point that Sanders requires a “case-specific application of judgment” is correct as far as it describes how harmless-error review is ordinarily performed, but it does not follow—textually—from § 7261(b)(2) that the Veterans Court is forbidden to rely on general, experience-based inferences about recurring errors when the record makes nonprejudice apparent. Kotteakos’s “substantial influence/grave doubt” test is itself a practical, record-focused standard, and it permits affirmance where the existing record shows the defect could not have affected the outcome; it does not demand a remand simply because an error falls within a procedural category. Justice Barrett’s concern about “categorical harmlessness” has bite only if the lower court treats the category as irrebuttable and refuses to look at the record; but if the court actually examines the record and concludes this type of error, on these facts, made no difference, that is faithful to the text’s command to “take due account” of prejudicial error. I therefore remain with Justice Alito: Sanders rejects rigid presumptions, but it does not constitutionalize or statutory-ize a requirement of individualized remand analysis in every case where a procedural misstep is identified.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right that Sanders speaks of a “case-specific application of judgment,” and I agree the Veterans Court may not adopt a rigid, across-the-board rule that bypasses the record entirely. But Justice Thomas correctly emphasizes that § 7261(b)(2)’s text incorporates ordinary harmless-error principles, and ordinary practice permits appellate courts to recognize recurring errors that are almost always nonprejudicial so long as the conclusion is justified by what the record shows in the case at hand. Under Kotteakos’s practical inquiry into effect, the key is whether the error likely influenced the outcome; requiring a formalized issue-by-issue remand analysis even when harmlessness is apparent risks recreating the remand-tilting rigidity Sanders rejected. The proper constraint is not a categorical ban on generalizations, but a requirement that any inference of harmlessness remain tethered to the particular record rather than operating as an irrebuttable presumption.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2) does not demand remand for every defect and permits affirmance when the record shows the error made no difference, and I accept that much. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sanders’s instruction of a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record” forecloses the Veterans Court from using a categorical harmlessness rule that effectively presumes entire classes of notice or duty-to-assist errors are nonprejudicial. Justice Alito’s cost and workability concerns are real, yet Kotteakos already supplies a practical filter—affirmance where harmlessness is apparent—without insulating recurring procedural failures that most harm veterans least able to develop evidence. The prejudice inquiry must remain individualized because duty-to-assist errors can distort what evidence exists in the record, making class-based assumptions particularly unreliable and unfair to vulnerable claimants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2)’s text—“take due account of the rule of prejudicial error”—does not require automatic remands or any ritualized, issue-by-issue write-up when harmlessness is clear from the record. But Chief Justice Roberts correctly emphasizes Sanders’s “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” which means the Veterans Court cannot replace that judgment with a categorical rule that a class of notice/duty-to-assist errors is harmless “in operation.” Justice Alito’s systemic-cost concern is real, yet Kotteakos/Sanders already provide a workable off-ramp: swift affirmance when the record shows no substantial influence (or no grave doubt), without converting that practical intuition into a presumption that forecloses individualized prejudice analysis. A narrow vacatur/remand requiring record-grounded harmless-error reasoning preserves statutory coherence—no pro-veteran presumption of prejudice, and no mirror-image presumption of harmlessness either.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2)’s text does not mandate remand for every error and, consistent with Sanders, permits affirmance when the record shows no effect. But his and Justice Alito’s move toward treating certain “classes of errors” as effectively nonprejudicial risks the very kind of rigid, non-record-based framework Sanders rejected—only with the presumption flipped—and it sits uneasily with Kotteakos’s insistence that harmlessness turns on whether the error had a substantial influence (or leaves grave doubt) in the particular proceeding. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Sanders requires a case-specific application of judgment based on examination of the record; that standard is fully compatible with efficient affirmance when harmlessness is apparent, but not with categorical shortcuts that bypass the inquiry. Textually, “take due account” calls for a genuine, record-grounded prejudicial-error analysis, not a judge-made safe harbor for recurring agency procedural violations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that § 7261(b)(2)’s text does not demand automatic remand and permits affirmance when the record makes nonprejudice clear, and I agree with that baseline. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Sanders’s controlling instruction is a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” which rules out the Veterans Court converting recurring-error experience into a categorical harmlessness rule that forecloses individualized analysis. Justice Alito’s administrative-cost concern is real, yet Kotteakos/Sanders already provides a practical mechanism for swift affirmance where harmlessness is obvious without creating a de facto safe harbor for recurring VA procedural lapses. Under an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, the cleanest course is a narrow vacatur requiring an issue- and record-specific harmless-error assessment rather than a class-based presumption of harmlessness.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the text of § 7261(b)(2) does not compel remand for every procedural defect and that ordinary harmless-error principles permit affirmance when nonprejudice is clear. But Sanders’s controlling instruction—emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—requires a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” and it rejects “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules,” which includes a categorical harmlessness rule that forecloses that inquiry. Justice Alito’s point about recurring errors is persuasive only if it operates as a rebuttable, record-confirmed inference in the particular case; once treated as a class-wide shortcut, it becomes the mirror-image presumption Sanders disapproved and risks evading Kotteakos’s substantial-influence/grave-doubt framework. The appropriate disposition is therefore a narrow vacatur to require the Veterans Court to explain harmlessness on this record, not a rule that effectively immunizes a category of errors from meaningful prejudice review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2) imports ordinary harmless-error review and does not compel remand for every procedural misstep, and Justice Alito fairly underscores the systemic costs of reflexive remands. But under Sanders and Kotteakos, “ordinary” harmless-error doctrine requires a record-grounded, case-specific judgment about substantial influence or grave doubt—not a rule that particular notice/duty-to-assist errors are harmless in operation, especially where the very consequence of the error may be an underdeveloped record. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, allowing categorical harmlessness risks flipping Sanders’s rejection of rigid presumptions into a mirror-image rigidity that dilutes Congress’s procedural safeguards in a uniquely claimant-protective system. A remand limited to requiring an issue- and record-specific harmlessness analysis preserves practicality while ensuring procedural fairness and attention to real-world consequences.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) instructs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which Shinseki v. Sanders interprets to require the ordinary harmless-error inquiry—a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” not the use of rigid, mandatory presumptions. 556 U.S. 396, 406–07 (2009). While Sanders rejects special pro-veteran presumptions and places the burden of showing prejudice on the appellant in the usual way, it also cautions against categorical harmlessness rules that bypass the record-based assessment whether the particular notice or duty-to-assist error affected the outcome. A narrow disposition would therefore vacate to the extent the Veterans Court treated such errors as categorically harmless and require an issue-specific harmless-error analysis consistent with § 7261(b)(2) and Kotteakos’s substantial-rights framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which incorporates the ordinary harmless-error principle rather than mandating remand for every notice or duty-to-assist defect. In Shinseki v. Sanders, 556 U.S. 396 (2009), this Court rejected “complex, rigid, and mandatory” presumptions in veterans cases and held § 7261(b)(2) requires the same kind of harmless-error analysis courts apply in civil cases—one that permits affirmance when the record shows no effect on the outcome. Nothing in the statute’s text requires an issue-specific inquiry in every case or forbids the court from concluding, based on the nature of the error and the record, that certain classes of errors are nonprejudicial in operation. Consistent with Kotteakos v. United States, 328 U.S. 750 (1946), reversal is warranted only where the error had a “substantial and injurious effect,” and the Veterans Court may apply that standard without adopting petitioner’s remand-leaning regime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which Shinseki v. Sanders held incorporates the ordinary civil harmless-error rule rather than a “complex, rigid, and mandatory” remand regime. 556 U.S. at 406-07. Ordinary harmless-error doctrine permits affirmance when the record shows the mistake made no difference, and it does not forbid courts from recognizing recurring classes of errors that are predictably nonprejudicial so long as the conclusion rests on record-based judgment in the case. Requiring an issue-specific inquiry in every instance would risk turning § 7261(b)(2) into a near-automatic remand rule, with substantial practical costs to the benefits system and little gain where the record demonstrates harmlessness.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which, as Shinseki v. Sanders explains, calls for a case-specific application of judgment based on examination of the record—not categorical shortcuts that presume entire classes of notice or duty-to-assist errors are harmless. While Sanders rejected “complex, rigid, and mandatory” presumptions that automatically favor remand, it equally confirms that harmless-error review must be grounded in the particular veteran’s circumstances and the likely effect of the error on developing evidence or presenting the claim. Categorical nonprejudice rules risk diluting the pro-claimant structure of the veterans benefits system and, in practical effect, shift the consequences of VA’s procedural failures onto veterans least able to overcome them. Consistent with Kotteakos and ordinary harmless-error principles incorporated by § 7261(b)(2), the Veterans Court must ask whether the specific error had a “substantial influence” on the outcome in the individual case before denying relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which this Court in Shinseki v. Sanders construed to require the ordinary harmless-error inquiry: a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” not “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules.” 556 U.S. at 406-07. While Sanders rejects a pro-veteran regime of automatic presumptions of prejudice, it equally disfavors the mirror-image approach—categorically deeming certain notice/duty-to-assist errors harmless without asking whether, in the circumstances, the error could have affected the claimant’s ability to develop evidence or obtain benefits. Consistent with Kotteakos and the statute’s text, the Veterans Court may affirm where the record shows no harm, but it must reach that conclusion through an issue- and record-specific harmless-error analysis rather than a categorical shortcut.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2) requires the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which, as Shinseki v. Sanders explained, means applying the ordinary harmless-error inquiry that entails a “case-specific application of judgment” on the record rather than “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules.” 556 U.S. 396, 406–07 (2009). A categorical rule deeming particular notice or duty-to-assist violations harmless without an issue- and record-specific assessment risks substituting a judicially crafted presumption for the statute’s instruction and undermines the separation-of-powers principle that courts may not rewrite Congress’s chosen standard of review. Consistent with Kotteakos v. United States, the proper question is whether the error had a substantial influence in the particular case; that cannot be answered by across-the-board assumptions divorced from the veteran’s circumstances. 328 U.S. 750, 764–65 (1946).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which this Court in Shinseki v. Sanders interpreted to require the ordinary harmless-error inquiry—a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” rather than “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules.” 556 U.S. at 406-08. Categorical harmlessness rules for classes of VA notice/duty-to-assist errors risk reintroducing the kind of rigid framework Sanders rejected and can undermine practical workability by preventing the court from assessing whether the error mattered in the particular veteran’s case. Consistent with Kotteakos and traditional harmless-error principles, the better reading is that prejudice must be assessed in context, even if in some cases the record will make harmlessness readily apparent without a remand.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” a phrase that, in ordinary legal usage, calls for a harmless-error inquiry tethered to the record and the particular proceeding rather than a blanket declaration that an entire class of errors never matters. Shinseki v. Sanders held that § 7261(b)(2) incorporates the ordinary civil harmless-error rule and emphasized its “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” rejecting “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules.” 556 U.S. at 406–07. A categorical rule deeming certain notice/duty-to-assist errors harmless without an issue-specific inquiry risks recreating the kind of rigid framework Sanders disapproved and is difficult to reconcile with the statutory instruction to take “due account” in the course of review under § 7261(a). Kotteakos reinforces that harmless-error review turns on whether the error had “substantial and injurious effect or influence” in the particular case, not on abstract assumptions about error categories.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which, as Shinseki v. Sanders explains, means applying ordinary harmless-error principles through a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” not via rigid presumptions. Allowing VA notice or duty-to-assist errors to be deemed categorically harmless risks short-circuiting that statutory command and undermines procedural fairness in a pro-claimant system where such errors can practically affect a veteran’s ability to develop evidence and present arguments. Consistent with Kotteakos, the proper inquiry is whether the particular error had “substantial influence” on the outcome (or leaves grave doubt), which requires attention to the individual circumstances rather than broad assumptions. A contextual, issue-specific analysis better aligns with equal-protection and criminal-justice-adjacent fairness concerns by preventing systemic burdens from falling on the least resourced claimants.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2)’s command that the Veterans Court “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error” requires case-specific harmless-error review, or instead permits the Veterans Court to treat certain veterans-law errors as categorically harmless without examining whether the particular claimant was harmed.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 7261 (especially § 7261(a) and § 7261(b)(2) governing the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims’ scope of review and its duty to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Federal Circuit has allowed (and in practice required) the Veterans Court to apply an overly rigid harmless-error framework that can deem VA/Board errors nonprejudicial as a category rather than evaluating prejudice in the individual veteran’s case, contrary to the text and purpose of § 7261(b)(2) and ordinary administrative-law harmless-error principles. They contend the Veterans Court must conduct a record-based, case-specific prejudice inquiry—asking whether the error could have affected the outcome or the fairness of the proceeding—rather than foreclosing relief through categorical no-prejudice rules that systematically disadvantage veterans in a uniquely claimant-friendly benefits system.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues that § 7261(b)(2) incorporates the traditional harmless-error principle and leaves the Veterans Court discretion to determine when an error is prejudicial, including using settled, administrable rules for recurring contexts. In the government’s view, the Federal Circuit’s approach is consistent with how appellate courts generally handle harmless error: the claimant typically must explain how the alleged error mattered on the facts, and courts need not remand for errors that could not have affected the outcome. The respondent also emphasizes that the Veterans Court already reviews the full record and can (and does) grant relief when an error is plausibly outcome-affecting, so no special, veteran-specific prejudice regime is required beyond § 7261(b)(2)’s ordinary “due account” instruction.
key_precedents: Shinseki v. Sanders, 556 U.S. 396 (2009) (harmless error / prejudicial error in veterans cases; burden and case-specific inquiry)
Kotteakos v. United States, 328 U.S. 750 (1946) (classic harmless-error formulation often used by analogy)
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706 (background harmless-error principle in administrative review, often referenced in veterans-law harmless-error discussions)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan make the strongest case that Sanders requires a "case-specific application of judgment" and that categorical harmlessness can harden into the very rigid presumptions Sanders condemned; that caution is well taken. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 7261(b)(2) incorporates ordinary harmless-error review, which permits administrable recurring principles so long as they do not displace record-based judgment; Sanders rejected "complex, rigid, and mandatory" frameworks, not reasoned conclusions that an error was incapable of affecting the outcome under the governing law and this record. I would therefore affirm on the narrow ground that the Veterans Court may rely on recurring harmless-error guideposts only if it explains—tethered to the record and governing law—why there is no plausible path to prejudice here, policing the line against per se no-prejudice shortcuts without imposing a remand ritual. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about shifting the costs of error onto veterans is real, but it is answered by requiring a genuine, articulated record-based harmlessness determination rather than forbidding administrable harmless-error principles altogether.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Sanders repeatedly speaks of a “case-specific application of judgment” and warns against rigid presumptions, but under a textualist reading that language polices method, not outcomes: § 7261(b)(2) commands the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” a phrase that incorporates the ordinary harmless-error inquiry, which has long permitted administrable conclusions that certain errors cannot affect results under governing law. Justice Sotomayor is right that courts may not treat labels as substitutes for analysis, yet the statute does not require a prejudice ritual where the record and law already foreclose any plausible prejudice; the constraint is that the court must be tethered to the record and legal framework, not that it must deny the existence of recurring harmless-error principles. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly identify the narrow line Sanders drew—rejecting “complex, rigid, and mandatory” frameworks—not forbidding record-grounded determinations of outcome-irrelevance. I therefore would affirm for Respondent while emphasizing that any harmlessness determination must be explained with reference to the governing law and the record, so administrability does not ossify into an irrebuttable presumption.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the strongest objection: Sanders’s “case-specific application of judgment” language risks being nullified if the Veterans Court can treat recurring error types as per se harmless. But I read Sanders, as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas do, to reject only “complex, rigid, and mandatory” presumptions that displace judgment—not to forbid the ordinary harmless-error conclusion that an error was incapable of affecting the outcome under the governing law and the established record. Section 7261(b)(2)’s command to “take due account” incorporates that conventional appellate practice, which has long allowed courts to identify situations where the error could not have mattered, so long as the court explains why on this record rather than relying on an abstract label. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about shifting the costs of agency error is policy-salient, but it cannot justify converting § 7261(b)(2) from a limitation on remands into a remand mandate whenever an error fits a recurring type, even when the record forecloses prejudice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that ordinary harmless-error doctrine can employ administrable guideposts—does not answer the core problem here: when a “guidepost” operates as a categorical no-prejudice rule, it ceases to be a record-based judgment and becomes the kind of rigid shortcut Sanders rejected. Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2) restrains remands for nonprejudicial error, but “nonprejudicial” still has to be demonstrated from the governing law and this veteran’s record, not inferred from an error’s label in the abstract. Justice Alito’s systemic-burden concerns are real, yet in a veteran-friendly scheme we cannot shift the costs of agency error onto individual claimants by presuming away plausible prejudice without explaining how the error could not have mattered here. I remain aligned with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett: permit recurring principles, but require a reasoned, record-tethered harmlessness explanation—something the approach below fails to demand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that Sanders imported ordinary harmless-error review and did not categorically ban administrable guideposts; I agree, and I would not read § 7261(b)(2) to require a pointless “prejudice ritual” when governing law and record facts show an error truly could not matter. But Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s framing risks letting the “guidepost” do the whole job: if the Veterans Court can declare an error-type outcome-irrelevant without explaining—by reference to this record—why there was no plausible path to a different result, the inquiry becomes the kind of rigid, outcome-determinative shortcut Sanders rejected. Textually, the trigger remains whether the error was “prejudicial” in this case, and pragmatically the workable middle ground is to allow recurring principles only as aids to a record-tethered explanation, not as per se no-prejudice rules that bypass case-specific judgment. Because the approach defended by Respondent does not sufficiently police that line, I stay with Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest opposing point: Sanders allows “administrable” harmless-error principles and does not demand an individualized “ritual” where the governing law and record show the error could not matter. But that framing still assumes what must be shown—harmlessness “on this record”—and it cannot justify a categorical no-prejudice rule that resolves prejudice in the abstract, untethered to the veteran’s evidentiary posture and the legal standards actually applied below. Justice Thomas is right that § 7261(b)(2) limits remands, yet the way the statute implements that limitation is by taking “due account” of prejudicial error in a case-specific, record-examining manner; per se harmlessness risks becoming the kind of rigid shortcut Sanders rejected. Under a textualist/originalist approach attentive to separation-of-powers limits, courts may not rewrite Congress’s record-bound prejudice inquiry into categorical immunity for whole classes of agency error simply for administrability’s sake.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a recurring “harmlessness” guidepost can harden into the kind of rigid, de facto presumption Sanders rejected, especially in a veteran-friendly system. But I read Sanders (as the Chief Justice does) to condemn “complex, rigid, and mandatory” frameworks that displace judgment, not to forbid courts from using administrable principles when the governing law and this record show the error could not have affected the outcome; ordinary harmless-error practice has long permitted that. The right constraint—addressing Justice Sotomayor’s concern about skipping plausible prejudice—is to require the Veterans Court to explain, with record and law, why there is no plausible pathway from the error to a different result here, rather than adopting an across-the-board prohibition on recurring harmless-error determinations. Nothing in § 7261(b)(2)’s text (“take due account”) or Sanders’s incorporation of traditional harmless-error doctrine compels petitioner’s broader rule, so I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point for Respondent: ordinary harmless-error doctrine can include administrable principles, and § 7261(b)(2)’s “take due account” naturally incorporates that tradition. But Sanders (tracking Kotteakos) repeatedly insists that harmlessness requires “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” which is incompatible with a categorical no-prejudice rule that resolves prejudice in the abstract rather than by explaining why this error could not have affected this veteran’s outcome on this record. I accept the Chief Justice’s institutional concern about needless remands, yet his narrow path still demands a record-tethered explanation; what I cannot accept is treating an error label as outcome-irrelevant without articulating the causal impossibility (or lack of plausible effect) under governing law and the record as developed. Under my textualist/originalist approach, “due account” plus § 7261(a)’s record-limited review is best implemented by allowing guideposts only as aids to that record-based prejudice judgment, not as per se dispositive rules.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the best point for Respondent: § 7261(b)(2) and Sanders incorporate ordinary harmless-error doctrine, which can include administrable guideposts, and Sanders rejected only “complex, rigid, and mandatory” presumptions. But on my procedural-fairness, consequences-sensitive approach, that concession does not validate a categorical no-prejudice shortcut that avoids the Sanders-required “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” especially where the very procedural error may have skewed record development in a veteran-friendly system. Justice Alito’s delay concerns are substantial, yet insulating repeat agency errors through abstract harmlessness determinations risks systematically shifting the costs of mistakes onto veterans and undermining confidence in the process. I therefore stay with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett: guideposts are permissible, but the Veterans Court must explain—tethered to this record and this claimant—why the error could not have mattered.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to "take due account of the rule of prejudicial error," which this Court in Shinseki v. Sanders construed to require the ordinary harmless-error approach used in civil cases, rejecting only "complex, rigid, and mandatory" presumptions that displaced record-based judgment. Sanders emphasizes case-specific examination of the record, but it does not foreclose the Veterans Court from employing administrable, recurring harmless-error principles so long as they reflect the traditional inquiry whether the error could have affected the outcome. A narrow ruling preserving Sanders’ framework best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy: the Veterans Court must consider prejudice in light of the record, yet may treat some errors as harmless where, on the established record and governing law, the error could not have made a difference. Accordingly, I would affirm discretion for the Veterans Court consistent with § 7261(b)(2) and Sanders, without creating a veteran-specific, categorical anti-harmless-error rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which most naturally incorporates the ordinary harmless-error principle rather than mandating a bespoke, invariably case-by-case prejudice inquiry for every asserted error. In Shinseki v. Sanders, 556 U.S. 396 (2009), this Court held § 7261(b)(2) requires application of the same kind of harmless-error rule used in civil cases and rejected “complex, rigid, and mandatory” frameworks; nothing in the statute’s language forbids the Veterans Court from using administrable rules for recurring contexts so long as it applies the prejudicial-error rule. Section 7261(a) already cabins the Veterans Court’s review to specified determinations on the record, and § 7261(b)(2) functions as a limitation against remanding for nonprejudicial error, not as an affirmative command to conduct an individualized prejudice inquiry in every category of error. Because the statute’s original public meaning and Sanders align with ordinary appellate practice permitting harmlessness determinations where an error could not have affected the outcome, I would affirm the government’s position.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” language that naturally incorporates the ordinary harmless-error principle rather than mandating a special, veteran-specific, case-by-case prejudice ritual for every recurrent error type. In Shinseki v. Sanders, this Court rejected “complex, rigid, and mandatory” frameworks and held that § 7261(b)(2) calls for the same kind of harmless-error analysis used in civil cases, which permits administrable rules for errors that, as a practical matter, cannot affect the outcome on a given record. So long as the Veterans Court examines the record under § 7261(a) and does not apply conclusive presumptions that foreclose relief where prejudice is plausible, it may treat certain errors as categorically harmless when they are incapable of affecting the decision. Requiring individualized remands for errors that could not have mattered would burden the system and delay benefits without improving accuracy, a consequence Congress likely did not intend in adopting an ordinary prejudicial-error rule.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which, under Shinseki v. Sanders, means a record-based harmless-error inquiry requiring “case-specific application of judgment” rather than rigid, mandatory shortcuts. While Sanders rejected categorical presumptions that automatically favor veterans, it did not authorize categorical no-prejudice rules that systematically deny relief without asking whether the particular veteran was harmed by the agency’s error. Given the VA system’s remedial, claimant-friendly structure and Congress’s solicitude for veterans, the Veterans Court should not treat recurring errors as per se harmless when the error could plausibly affect the fairness or outcome for an individual claimant. Accordingly, § 7261(b)(2) is best read to require case-specific prejudice review, consistent with ordinary harmless-error principles and administrative-law review under 5 U.S.C. § 706.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which in context functions like the familiar harmless-error principle in administrative and civil review—one that ordinarily turns on a record-based assessment of whether the error mattered in the particular case. Shinseki v. Sanders held that § 7261(b)(2) calls for the “same kind of ‘harmless-error’ rule” used in civil cases and emphasized “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” rejecting “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules” that short-circuit that inquiry. While the Veterans Court may use administrable guideposts, it may not treat recurring veterans-law errors as categorically harmless when that dispenses with asking whether this claimant was actually harmed. A case-specific prejudice inquiry also better fits § 7261(a)’s instruction to decide legality and set aside unlawful actions, with § 7261(b)(2) operating as a limiting principle only when the error is truly nonprejudicial on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of § 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account” of the “rule of prejudicial error,” a phrase that—read in its ordinary legal sense—calls for application of the traditional harmless-error inquiry to the particular record rather than categorical, across-the-board declarations of harmlessness. Shinseki v. Sanders held that § 7261(b)(2) requires the same kind of harmless-error rule used in ordinary civil cases and emphasized a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record,” rejecting “complex, rigid, and mandatory” frameworks that displace that judgment. While courts may use general principles to guide analysis, separation-of-powers concerns counsel against judicially creating categorical no-prejudice rules that effectively rewrite the statutory command and risk denying relief without asking whether the veteran was actually harmed in his case. Accordingly, § 7261(b)(2) requires record-based, case-specific prejudicial-error review and does not permit categorical harmless-error treatment divorced from the claimant’s circumstances.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which this Court in Shinseki v. Sanders held incorporates the ordinary civil harmless-error rule rather than a “complex, rigid, and mandatory” veteran-specific framework. Sanders also emphasizes a “case-specific application of judgment” based on the record, but that language is best read to forbid mandatory presumptions—not to prohibit the Veterans Court from using administrable, recurring rules to identify errors that could not have affected the outcome. Consistent with traditional harmless-error principles (see Kotteakos) and the APA background (5 U.S.C. § 706), the Veterans Court may employ workable categorical guides so long as it remains tethered to whether an error was capable of causing prejudice in the case at hand. Given the institutional need for a practical, uniform system in high-volume veterans litigation, I would not read § 7261(b)(2) to categorically bar such administrable harmless-error rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 38 U.S.C. § 7261(b)(2) directs the Veterans Court to “take due account of the rule of prejudicial error,” which, as Shinseki v. Sanders construed it, means applying the ordinary civil harmless-error rule through a “case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record.” 556 U.S. 396, 406–07 (2009). That understanding is reinforced by § 7261’s structure: subsection (a) sets out record-based review, and subsection (b)(2) adds an obligation to evaluate whether identified error actually prejudiced the claimant, not to declare entire classes of errors harmless without looking at the particular record. To the extent categorical harmless-error rules function like “mandatory presumptions and rigid rules,” Sanders disapproved that approach and favors individualized harmless-error analysis consistent with Kotteakos’s outcome-affecting inquiry. Accordingly, § 7261(b)(2) requires case-specific harmless-error review rather than categorical no-prejudice determinations untethered to the claimant’s circumstances.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 7261(b)(2)’s instruction that the Veterans Court "take due account of the rule of prejudicial error" is best read, consistent with the APA’s background harmless-error principle (5 U.S.C. § 706), to require a record-based, case-specific inquiry into whether an identified VA/Board error could have affected the outcome or the fundamental fairness of the proceeding, rather than allowing categorical no-prejudice shortcuts. Shinseki v. Sanders emphasized that harmless-error review demands "case-specific application of judgment, based upon examination of the record," and rejected "complex, rigid, and mandatory" frameworks that function like presumptions rather than genuine prejudice analysis. Allowing whole classes of veterans-law errors to be deemed harmless without examining the individual claimant’s circumstances risks undermining procedural fairness in a uniquely claimant-protective system and can entrench practical, systemic disadvantage for veterans seeking benefits. The Veterans Court may use administrable guideposts, but § 7261(b)(2) does not permit rules that foreclose individualized prejudice determinations where the record could plausibly show harm.
